ece-01.title: Characteristics of Early Childhood
explain: **Early childhood** refers to the period before children enter school, roughly ages 3 to 5. Countries and school systems set the range differently, so age is only an approximate guide. **Early childhood education** is the field that studies how children in this period develop and learn. This course introduces theory only and does not cover licensing or field practicum.

Several features are often cited when describing children of this age. The first is **individual differences**. Many things change in a short time during this period, but when and how fast they change varies a great deal from child to child. Even children of the same age spread out over a wide range in the time at which they master a given skill.

explain.alt: Horizontal bars for three hypothetical children, Harin, Doyun, and Seoa, showing when each first cut along a line with scissors. The horizontal axis runs from age 3 to age 5. Harin's bar starts a little after age 3 and ends around age 3 and a half. Doyun's bar starts just before age 4 and ends a little after age 4. Seoa's bar runs from about age 4 and a half to age 5. Below the bars is written: each bar shows the span from the earliest to the latest time.
explain.caption: The age at which a skill is first mastered differs from child to child, and the timing spreads over a range.

explain: The second is **concrete, sensory understanding**. Young children tend to understand things by touching and moving the objects in front of them. Counting is often easier to grasp when they hand out one cup at a time than when numbers are only spoken aloud.

The third is a tendency toward an **egocentric perspective**. Piaget described the difficulty young children have in seeing that others may view things differently from themselves as egocentrism. Later studies showed that children can take another's perspective earlier when the situation is familiar, so this is best understood as a tendency rather than a fixed trait that every child shows at the same age.

The fourth is **holistic development**. Physical, language, cognitive, and emotional development do not proceed separately; they happen together within a single activity. Finally, early childhood is a time of exploring the world through **play and relationships**. These features form the background for the lessons that follow.

examples.title: A hypothetical classroom, before lunch on the same day
body: In the Sunshine Class (hypothetical), two four-year-olds take part in the same activity. Harin cuts out a shape by following a line on a sheet of paper, while Doyun, sitting beside her, is still learning how to hold the scissors. The two children are the same age but can do different things at this point. This is not a sign that one is better; it is one example of individual differences.

Later that day, Doyun builds a house with blocks and talks with a friend about the shape of the roof. Moving his body, thinking about shapes, speaking, and feeling pleasure or frustration all happen at once. This is an example of holistic development.

ece-02.title: Play and Learning
explain: **Play** is an activity in which a child chooses freely, enjoys it, and values the process itself more than the result. The features most often cited for play are voluntariness, enjoyment, a focus on process, and an element of imagination, such as "pretending." The weaker these features are, the closer an activity comes to a task rather than play.
Play can be divided in several ways. Here we introduce one widely used classification, which sorts play into four types according to what the play looks like.

- **Functional play**: repeating the same movement with the body or with objects, for enjoyment.
- **Constructive play**: building or making something with blocks, sand, clay, and the like.
- **Symbolic play**: treating one object or person as another and pretending.
- **Rule-based play**: understanding and following set rules and enjoying them.

explain.alt: Four lines showing four types of play. Functional play repeats the same movement; for example, rolling a ball and catching it again. Constructive play builds or makes something; for example, stacking blocks into a tower. Symbolic play pretends that something is something else; for example, serving tea in an empty cup. Rule-based play follows set rules; for example, taking turns in a card game.

explain: A single child's play rarely stays within one type. A child who stacks blocks (constructive) and then calls the tower a castle and starts a story (symbolic) moves between types. It is also said that younger children tend to do more functional and constructive play, and older children more rule-based play, although this differs from child to child.

Play is also where learning happens. Within play, children meet problems on their own (the tower falls over), use language (they assign roles), and agree with friends (they set the rules). Meanwhile, how to balance play with activities led by teachers is still an ongoing discussion, and no single view has been settled as correct.

During play, when they ask and answer "Where does it hurt?", language is being used, and when one suggests switching roles, "When my turn ends, you're the doctor," they are creating rules. The children did not play in order to learn, yet many things are being used within the play.

ece-03.title: Developmental Domains
explain: **Development** is the process by which a child's physical and mental abilities change over time. To make a child's changes easier to understand, they are often divided into several **domains**. This course uses four domains.

- **Physical development**: includes gross motor skills, which use large body movements (running, jumping), fine motor skills, which use the fingers (picking up small things, cutting with scissors), and the senses.
- **Cognitive development**: the ability to think, remember, and solve problems, and to understand numbers and size.
- **Language development**: the ability to understand others' speech and to express one's own thoughts in words.
- **Social-emotional development**: recognizing and managing one's own and others' feelings, and forming relationships with friends.

explain.alt: A diagram in which a central circle labeled as the whole child is linked by lines to four boxes. Upper-left box: physical, running and picking things up with the hands. Upper-right box: cognitive, counting, comparing, and solving problems. Lower-left box: language, listening and speaking. Lower-right box: social-emotional, recognizing feelings and friendships. At the bottom is written: the domains are not separate from one another; they are connected.

explain: How the domains are divided differs from source to source. Some place emotion apart from sociality, and others set artistic expression or morality apart. Domains are tools to aid understanding; they do not mean that a child has literal partitions inside.

So reading an activity through just one domain is often not enough. You can say which domain seems most prominent in an activity, but the key point of this lesson is not to overlook that the other domains are also being used together.

body: In the Rainbow Class (hypothetical), two children build a long bridge with blocks. Picking up and fitting the blocks with their hands is physical development, and judging how long each block should be is cognitive development.

Saying "You take this side, and I'll take that side" is language development, and when the bridge collapses and one child is upset but then suggests trying again, this connects to social-emotional development. A single scene contains all four domains.

ece-04.title: Environment Setup
explain: In early childhood education, the space and materials where children spend their time are called the **environment**, and the environment is seen as influencing children's play and learning. The environment is sometimes compared to "another teacher." The idea is that which materials are placed where, and how, changes what children want to do.

The spaces in a classroom divided by the kind of play they support are called **interest areas**. Common examples are the building area (blocks), the role-play area (house, shop), the art area, the manipulative area (puzzles, fitting toys), and the book area. Which areas to set up depends on the class and the space.

explain.alt: A bird's-eye view of a rectangular classroom layout. In the upper row, from left: the building area (may be noisy), the role-play area (shared play), and the art area (making things by hand). In the lower center is a meeting space drawn with dotted lines (where everyone gathers). In the lower left is the manipulative area (puzzles, fitting toys), and in the lower right is the book area (quiet looking). On the lower-left wall there is an orange door symbol.

explain: Several principles are often used when thinking about the arrangement.

- **Nature of activities**: noisy, movement-heavy areas and quiet, focused areas are kept apart, which reduces disruption.
- **Traffic flow**: leave paths so that children moving between areas do not cross through other children's play.
- **Accessibility**: place materials at child height so children can take them out and put them back on their own.
- **Flexibility**: keep some open space for gathering together or for play that grows, and change the arrangement when needed.

These principles are a framework for reading and thinking about an arrangement. There is no single correct layout; the same principles can lead different classes to different arrangements. This course does not cover safety standards or facility guidelines.

examples.title: A hypothetical classroom where the arrangement was reconsidered
body: In the Starlight Class (hypothetical), the book area was right next to the building area. Children reading books often moved away because of the noise when the blocks fell. The teacher decided to move the book area to a corner on the opposite side of the room.

After the move, the teacher kept watching to see whether the same problem had decreased, and if it had not, considered another approach. Arranging the environment is not a one-time task but a matter of adjusting it while watching how the children behave.

ece-05.title: Observation Records
explain: **Observation** is watching what a child does with a purpose, and an **observation record** is that observation written down. It serves as evidence for understanding the child and as the basis for deciding how to continue the play and the environment.

There are several observation methods. An **anecdotal record** briefly describes one event, a **checklist** confirms whether predetermined items appeared, and **time sampling** marks what the child is doing at fixed intervals. This lesson focuses on anecdotal records.
The most important thing in a record is to **separate fact from interpretation**. Facts are what was actually seen and heard; interpretation is what one thinks about it.

explain.alt: A diagram titled "Two columns of an observation record." Two columns, "What was seen and heard" on the left and "What was thought" on the right, are linked by arrows in three rows. Row 1: "Minjun rebuilt the tower after it fell" leads to "He is a persistent child." Row 2: "He held out one block to the friend beside him" leads to "He likes his friend." Row 3: "He said, Oh, fell again" leads to "He seems disappointed." At the bottom is written: "An interpretation is only one of several possible explanations."

explain: A factual record includes when, where, who, and what they did, as well as the words spoken, written as they were said. Words that carry evaluation or guesswork, such as "good," "restless," or "was angry," are interpretations, so they are not written in the fact column. Interpretations go in a separate column, with the reminder that they are one possible explanation.

There is a reason for separating the two. People read the same scene differently depending on first impressions or expectations. If facts and interpretations are mixed, a later reader will treat the interpretation as fact and easily judge the whole child from a single scene. Gathering records across several days and scenes makes the interpretations more solid.

examples.title: Splitting a mixed record into two columns (hypothetical)
body: Mixed record: "Juah played happily in the building area. She gave up her block to a friend."

- Fact: At 10:05, Juah placed one block in front of the friend beside her. Juah laughed out loud.
- Interpretation: Juah may want to play together with her friend.
"Happily" and "gave up" are words that mix in interpretation. Writing them separately also leaves room for readers to consider other interpretations.

ece-06.title: Observation Practice
explain: In this lesson you practice applying what you have learned to a hypothetical scene. Rather than observing a real child or classroom, you read and practice with a situation given in pictures and text.

Here is the order for observation practice. First, gather the **things seen and heard** in the scene in time order. Next, check whether there are any **words mixed with interpretation**. Finally, if you write an interpretation, separate it from the facts and also consider other possible explanations.

Three lines below: 10:20, Ga fills the bucket with sand using a shovel. 10:22, Na holds out the shovel to Ga, and Ga accepts it. 10:24, Da watches the two children from outside the pit, without speaking.

explain: When writing records, there are words to watch for. Evaluations, whether positive or negative ("well," "badly," "kindly"), words that assume what someone inwardly wants ("because they wanted to," "because they felt upset"), and words that exaggerate ("always," "never") often signal that interpretation has crept in. In the fact column, rewrite such words as the behaviors and words actually observed.

The records in this lesson do not evaluate or diagnose any child. Ga, Na, and Da are hypothetical children, and the most important lesson of this practice is that very little can be said about a child from a single scene.

There are many possible explanations. Da may be waiting for a turn, may find the play interesting to watch, or may be waiting for another game to end. Interpretation means listing several such explanations and then moving on to later scenes to check them.

ece-07.title: Piaget's Schemes and the Sensorimotor Stage
explain: In Stage 1 we saw that the characteristics of early childhood include an egocentric perspective and concrete, sensory understanding. But why do children understand the world this way? The Swiss scholar **Piaget** saw children not as containers that simply take in knowledge, but as beings who **construct** frameworks of understanding by bumping against the world themselves. This view is called **constructivism**.

The basic unit of Piaget's theory is the **scheme** (schema). A scheme is a framework of action or thought for understanding and dealing with the world. A baby's sucking or grasping, or an older child's idea that "a four-legged animal is a doggie," are all schemes. Schemes change in two ways.
- **Assimilation**: taking in a new experience by fitting it into an existing scheme. This is when a child sees a cat and calls it a "doggie."
- **Accommodation**: when an existing scheme does not fit, changing it or creating a new one. This is when a child begins to think, "The one that says meow is a cat," and separates the two.

When a child meets an experience that cannot be explained by assimilation, the child feels an uncomfortable mismatch, called **disequilibrium**. When a better scheme is created through accommodation, the child returns to a stable state, called **equilibrium**. Piaget called this process **equilibration** and saw it as the force that drives cognitive development. In short, the cycle of "assimilation, mismatch (disequilibrium), accommodation, new equilibrium" repeats, and schemes become more refined.

Piaget divided development into four stages: the **sensorimotor stage** (roughly birth to age 2), the **preoperational stage** (ages 2 to 7), the **concrete operational stage** (ages 7 to 11), and the **formal operational stage** (after age 11). The ages are rough guides; the order is the key point. A child in the sensorimotor stage knows the world through the senses and movement: seeing, hearing, touching, and moving. Piaget divided this stage further into six substages.
1. Reflex activity: using innate reflexes such as sucking and grasping.
2. Primary circular reactions: repeating one's own bodily action that happened by chance (sucking a finger).
3. Secondary circular reactions: repeating an interesting result that happened to an outside object (the sound of a rattle).
4. Coordination of secondary schemes: linking schemes to reach a goal (removing a cover to grab a toy).
5. Tertiary circular reactions: changing actions and experimenting with the results (dropping an object from different heights).
6. Beginning of mental representation: imagining actions in one's head, and deferred imitation, in which a child copies an action seen earlier.

The most famous achievement of the sensorimotor stage is **object permanence**, the understanding that an object continues to exist even when it cannot be seen. In Piaget's observations, very young infants did not search for a toy covered with a cloth. Around stage 4, children search for a covered toy, but a pattern appears in which, after finding the toy several times at location A, they search at A again even after it is moved to location B in front of them. This is called the **A-not-B error**. Object permanence becomes firmer in later stages.

The limits are also clear. Later research using more sensitive methods, such as measuring how long infants look at something, has reported that infants respond as if they anticipate an object's existence at an earlier age than Piaget observed. There is also criticism that development does not change in steps all at once at each stage, but advances unevenly depending on the domain and the task. Still, the view of the child as an active constructor, and the concepts of assimilation and accommodation, remain basic terms in early childhood education.

examples.title: Distinguishing assimilation from accommodation
body: Condition (hypothetical): Seojin, age 2, calls every round thing a "ball." When she saw a tangerine she said "ball!" and tried to roll it, but the tangerine did not roll well. When she peeled the skin, she found it could be eaten.
Step 1: Calling the tangerine a "ball" and trying to roll it fits a new object into the existing ball scheme. This is assimilation.

Step 2: After the mismatch (disequilibrium) that it does not roll and can be eaten, if she says "a tangerine is something you eat" and divides the two names, she has revised the scheme. This is accommodation.
Interpretation: Assimilation and accommodation are not opposites but two wheels that turn together, and the mismatch between them is the occasion for learning.

examples.title: Reading the substages
body: Condition (hypothetical): At about 10 months, when a child watches an adult hide a ball behind a box, the child pushes the box aside and grabs the ball.
Step 1: The scheme of "moving the box aside" and the scheme of "grabbing" were linked together to reach a goal.
Step 2: This corresponds to the fourth substage, coordination of secondary schemes. Because the child found the hidden ball, object permanence is also appearing to some extent.
Interpretation: The same child might show an A-not-B error when the ball is moved to another place, so the stage should not be judged from a single scene.

ece-08.title: Thought in the Preoperational Stage: Symbols, Egocentrism, and Conservation
explain: A four-year-old is given the same amount of juice, poured into two identical cups. When one cup is poured into a tall, thin glass, the child insists that the thin glass holds more. Why does a child judge this way? Piaget called the thinking of children roughly ages 2 to 7 the **preoperational stage**, and described what children in this period can do and what they find difficult.

First, what children have become able to do. The greatest achievement of the preoperational stage is the **symbolic function**, the ability to represent one thing with another. Using words, drawing pictures, and pretending that a block is a telephone for a pretend call all come from this ability. The symbolic play we saw in Stage 1 rests on this ability.

Piaget also described the limits of thinking at this stage. An "operation" is a logical activity that can be reversed in the head, and the preoperational stage means that such operations are not yet established.
- **Egocentrism**: difficulty distinguishing another person's perspective from one's own. In a three-mountain task, Piaget reported that children asked to choose what a doll sitting opposite them sees tended to choose the view from their own side.
- **Animism**: believing that inanimate things, such as the sun, clouds, or toys, have minds and life.
- **Centration**: attending to only one prominent aspect among several.
- **Irreversibility**: being unable to mentally reverse the course of a change.

explain.alt: A picture titled "Liquid quantity conservation task (hypothetical scene)." Panel 1 on the left shows cups A and B, of the same size, filled with water to the same height, with the caption "They are the same." An orange arrow labeled "pour" leads to panel 2 on the right, labeled "B poured into a tall, thin cup C." Panel 2 shows cup A and a taller, thinner cup C whose water is higher than A's. Below is written: "The child says C has more. The water is higher." At the bottom: "What did the child look at to judge between the two cups?" and "Nothing was added or removed while pouring."

explain: The **conservation task** in the picture shows this limit well. **Conservation** is the understanding that when the shape or arrangement changes, the amount stays the same as long as nothing is added or taken away. The child in the picture attends only to the water's height (centration) and does not take into account that the cup has become narrower. Nor does the child recall that pouring C's water back into B returns it to the original state (irreversibility). Once in the concrete operational stage, children understand conservation by giving reasons such as "we didn't add or take away anything, so it's the same," "it's higher but thinner," or "if you pour it back, it's the same again." Understanding of conservation differs by type (liquid quantity, number, length, weight), and the age at which each is understood varies.

There are limits to this explanation as well. Later research reported that when the task is changed to a familiar scene or the questions are refined, children around age 4 are fairly good at understanding others' perspectives. It has also been pointed out that when the same question is asked twice, a child may take it to mean "change your answer." Therefore, the characteristics of the preoperational stage are best read not as a list of things children cannot do, but as tendencies of thinking that vary with the task and context.

examples.title: Reading a number conservation task
body: Condition (hypothetical): Six counters are laid out in two rows of the same length, and the child says "they're the same." Then the spacing of one row is widened so that it is longer, and the child says, "This one has more."
Step 1: The counters were not added or taken away, so the number is the same.
Step 2: The child attended only to the length of the row (centration). The child did not recall that gathering them up again makes them equal (irreversibility).
Interpretation: This can be read as a response in which number conservation is not yet established. However, when children are asked to count the counters themselves, some change their judgment.

examples.title: Distinguishing egocentrism from animism
body: Condition (hypothetical): (1) On the phone, a child tells her grandmother "Look at this!" and holds up her drawing in front of the receiver. (2) The child says, "The sun is following me."
Step 1: (1) shows the child assuming her grandmother can see what she sees, which can be read as egocentrism.
Step 2: (2) speaks as if the sun has the will to follow her, which can be read as animism.
Interpretation: Neither statement is simply a "wrong idea" but a clue to features of thinking at this stage, and neither should be judged from a single utterance.

checks.explanation: The symbolic function is an achievement, while the other three are limits of thinking that Piaget described.

ece-09.title: Vygotsky's ZPD, Scaffolding, Private Speech, and Executive Function
explain: Where Piaget portrayed a child who builds understanding alone by bumping against the world, the Russian scholar **Vygotsky** emphasized that children learn through activities shared with others. His view is called **sociocultural theory**. In it, ways of thinking themselves, carried by cultural tools such as language, first appear between people and then gradually move inside the child.

Vygotsky's central concept is the **zone of proximal development** (ZPD). It is the range between what a child can do alone and what the child can do with help from a more capable person. He saw the support that drives learning as most effective within this range, not in tasks the child can already do alone and not in tasks that remain hard even with help.

explain.alt: Concentric circles titled "One child's tasks seen in three zones." The innermost green circle reads "Can do alone." The middle ring with an orange border reads "Can do with help." The outermost gray ring reads "Still hard even with help." A legend on the right names the inner circle, middle ring, and outer ring, and says: "Boundaries are not fixed; they widen outward as learning progresses."

explain:
As the figure shows, a child's tasks can be seen in three zones. The middle ring is the zone of proximal development. The support given there is often called **scaffolding**, a metaphor for the temporary frame that is put up while a building is under construction and taken down when it is finished. The term spread widely after Vygotsky, through its use by Wood, Bruner, Ross, and others. Scaffolding can be summarized in the following sequence.
1. Observe how far the child can go alone right now.
2. Give only as much help as is needed, such as breaking the task down, asking a question, or demonstrating.
3. Reduce the help gradually to match what the child can do.
4. When the child can do it alone, withdraw the help and look for the next task at the widened boundary.

Vygotsky also paid attention to children's **private speech**, the talk they direct to themselves. Piaget regarded this as egocentric speech that disappears as social skills grow. Vygotsky saw it instead as a tool the child uses to guide and plan their own actions. The guiding words an adult once used become the child's private speech and later become silent **inner speech**. The observation that private speech increases when a task is difficult is often cited in support of this interpretation.

Private speech also connects to today's research on **executive function**. Executive function is a bundle of abilities for regulating thinking and behavior toward a goal, usually divided into three components.
- **Inhibition**: holding back a response one wants to make (waiting for a signal).
- **Working memory**: holding information in mind briefly and working with it (remembering three errands).
- **Cognitive flexibility**: changing rules or perspectives in thinking (sorting by color, then switching to sorting by shape).
For example, when children who have been sorting cards by color are told to switch to sorting by shape, many three-year-olds keep sorting by the old rule even while saying the new rule aloud. Such patterns decline considerably over early childhood.

There are limits and points of debate as well. The zone of proximal development is an attractive concept, but its range is difficult to measure precisely, and studies define "help" differently. Many views, rather than treating Vygotsky and Piaget as simply opposed, see a child's own exploration and social support working together. Executive function is not explained by age alone; it varies widely by task, situation, and individual.

examples.title: Reading scaffolding in a puzzle activity
body: Condition (hypothetical): Four-year-old Jiho completes a 12-piece puzzle alone, but when he tries a 24-piece puzzle alone he gives up partway. When the teacher asks, "Shall we look for the corner pieces first?" he finishes it. With a 100-piece puzzle, he loses interest quickly even with help.
Step 1: The 12-piece puzzle can be seen as within his solo ability, the 24-piece puzzle as one he can do with help, and the 100-piece puzzle as still hard.
Step 2: The task where scaffolding is most meaningful is the 24-piece puzzle. Next time, the teacher drops the question about the corners, watches, and gradually reduces the help.
Interpretation: If Jiho completes the 24-piece puzzle alone, the boundary has widened, and the tasks beyond it become the new zone of proximal development.

examples.title: Private speech and executive function
body: Condition (hypothetical): During a game of "Stop at the red light," a child mutters, "Red light, stop... stop..." and stops her body.
Step 1: Holding back the urge to run and stopping is related to inhibition, one aspect of executive function.
Step 2: From Vygotsky's perspective, the muttering can be read as private speech that guides her own behavior.
Interpretation: Rather than telling her to be quiet, one might consider that she is using private speech as a tool to regulate herself.

ece-10.title: Temperament and Goodness of Fit
explain: In the same classroom and the same activity, one child goes straight up to a new visitor while another stands at a distance and watches for a long time. Such differences are often not explained by parenting alone. A relatively stable tendency in reaction, which people have from birth and which appears fairly early and persists to a degree, is called **temperament**. Temperament forms the basis of personality but is not personality itself; it is shaped by experience.

The American psychiatrists **Thomas** and **Chess** followed many children from infancy over a long period (the New York Longitudinal Study) and divided temperament into nine dimensions.
- Activity level, rhythmicity (regularity of eating and sleeping), approach or withdrawal (whether the child moves toward new situations)
- Adaptability, intensity of reaction, mood (the ratio of cheerful to unpleasant mood)
- Attention span and persistence, distractibility, threshold of responsiveness (how weak a stimulus must be to produce a reaction)

Grouping these dimensions, they proposed three types.
- **Easy child**: regular daily rhythms, readily approaches new situations, and generally cheerful mood. About 40% of the study sample.
- **Difficult child**: irregular rhythms, avoids new situations, and reacts intensely. About 10%.
- **Slow-to-warm-up child** (a child who adapts slowly): initially withdraws from new situations but adapts over time, and tends to have mild reactions. About 15%.
The remaining 35% did not clearly fall into any type. The fact that more than a third of the children do not fit a type is a sign that temperament should not be treated as a fixed category.

A key concept that Thomas and Chess left behind is **goodness of fit**. A child's temperament is not good or bad in itself; how well it matches the demands of the environment and the expectations and responses of adults determines later adjustment. Even among slow-to-warm-up children, a child in an environment that gives time to watch before joining a new activity adjusts without difficulty, while in an environment that demands immediate participation, conflict can grow.

The steps for reading goodness of fit are as follows.
1. Describe the child's behavior in the language of the temperament dimensions (for example, initially withdraws from new situations).
2. Note what the environment demands (for example, large-group participation from the first day).
3. Find the points where the two do not match.
4. Before trying to change the child, first think about what the environment can adjust (for example, starting with small groups, or giving time to look around in advance).

There are limitations as well. Later researchers have divided temperament in other ways; for example, some models summarize it with fewer dimensions, such as negative emotionality, extraversion (activity and approach), and effortful control. Temperament is mainly measured through parent reports, so the reporter's viewpoint may enter the results, and what counts as desirable temperament differs across cultures. This lesson introduces a framework for understanding temperament only; it is not used to evaluate or diagnose any child.

examples.title: Reading goodness of fit
body: Condition (hypothetical): Daon, age 3, watches new games from a distance at first and then joins in happily after a few days. On the first day of the new school term, the teacher asked all the children to gather immediately in a large circle to sing, and Daon stood in a corner and cried.
Step 1: Daon's behavior resembles the pattern of a slow-to-warm-up child, who initially withdraws in a new situation but adapts over time. This is a description, not a label.

Step 2: The demand of the environment (immediate participation in a large group) did not match the child's tendency. Consider adjustments such as a place and time to watch, and starting with a small group.
Interpretation: The goodness-of-fit view looks for the cause of the problem in the degree of fit, rather than in a single trait of the child.

examples.title: Calculating type proportions
body: Condition: Apply Thomas and Chess's proportions (easy 40%, difficult 10%, slow-to-warm-up 15%, remainder 35%) directly to a hypothetical group of 200 children.
Step 1: Easy children: 200 × 0.40 = 80. Difficult children: 200 × 0.10 = 20. Slow-to-warm-up children: 200 × 0.15 = 30.
Step 2: Children who do not clearly fall into any type: 200 − 80 − 20 − 30 = 70.
Interpretation: This is only a calculation to understand the proportions. The actual proportions in any real group vary with the sample and the measurement method.

checks.explanation: The three types are summarized as combinations of the nine dimensions.

ece-11.title: Bowlby and Ainsworth's Attachment Theory
explain: Why does an infant cry when a particular person leaves, and go up to that person to be held when the person returns? In Stage 1 we described attachment simply as an emotional bond. In this lesson we look more deeply at the ideas of **Bowlby**, who established attachment theory, and **Ainsworth**, who created a method for observing the quality of attachment.

The British psychiatrist Bowlby explained attachment from an evolutionary perspective. The tendency of a helpless infant to stay close to a protective adult supported survival, and behaviors such as crying, smiling, following, and clinging maintain that closeness. The infant uses the attachment figure as a **secure base** for exploration, setting out to explore and returning when anxious to find comfort. Bowlby saw attachment as developing roughly in the following sequence.
1. Pre-attachment phase (roughly birth to 6 weeks): signals are sent to anyone, with no specific attachment yet.
2. Attachment-in-the-making phase (roughly 6 weeks to 6 to 8 months): the infant begins to respond differently to familiar people.
3. Clear-cut attachment phase (roughly 6 to 8 months to 18 months to 2 years): the infant seeks a particular person and shows separation anxiety when that person leaves.
4. Goal-corrected partnership phase (roughly 18 months to 2 years onward): with growing language and understanding, the child knows why the caregiver leaves and when they will return, and can negotiate.

Bowlby believed that accumulated attachment experiences produce an **internal working model**. These are mental frameworks of expectation about oneself and others, such as "other people help me when I'm in trouble" and "I am someone worth helping." He believed this framework can influence expectations and behavior in later relationships.

Ainsworth, an American, created the **Strange Situation** procedure to observe the quality of attachment in the laboratory. A child of roughly 12 to 18 months goes into an unfamiliar room with the caregiver, and in sequence experiences eight short scenes: a stranger enters, the caregiver leaves briefly, and then returns. Particularly important is the caregiver's behavior when they **return** (reunion). Based on this, Ainsworth proposed three types, and later Main and Solomon added a fourth.
- **Secure attachment**: may cry when separated, but upon reunion approaches happily, is comforted, and soon returns to exploring.
- **Insecure-avoidant attachment**: shows little response when separated, and upon reunion avoids or ignores the caregiver.
- **Insecure-resistant (ambivalent) attachment**: very distressed when separated, and upon reunion wants to be held yet pushes away angrily, and is not easily calmed.
- **Disorganized attachment**: shows no consistent pattern, such as approaching and then freezing.

explain.alt: A table titled "Strange Situation observation records (three hypothetical infants)." The columns are infant, when the caregiver leaves, and when the caregiver returns. Ga: when the caregiver leaves, cries and looks toward the door; when the caregiver returns, approaches and is held, soon calms, and returns to the toys. Na: when the caregiver leaves, keeps playing with no particular reaction; when the caregiver returns, looks away and does not approach. Da: when the caregiver leaves, cries hard; when the caregiver returns, wants to be held yet pushes away, and does not calm for a long time. At the bottom: "A record is a single observation and does not diagnose the child."

explain: The figure is a record of three hypothetical infants. The key point in reading such records is not to judge by crying during separation alone. Ga and Da both cry when separated, but at reunion Ga soon calms and plays again, while Da approaches yet pushes away and does not calm for a long time. Na did not cry during separation, but that does not necessarily mean the attachment is secure, because Na avoided the caregiver at reunion.

There are limitations and points of debate as well. The Strange Situation is a research procedure, and reactions vary with a child's temperament, the day's condition, and culture. For example, it has been pointed out that the meaning of the same behavior may differ between cultures where children rarely separate from caregivers and cultures where separation is common. Attachment can also form with several people, not only one caregiver. Attachment types are classifications for research; they should not be used to judge a child or family, or to diagnose from a single observation.

examples.title: Reading a secure base scene
body: Condition (hypothetical): At a playground the child has never visited, a one-year-old climbs down from the caregiver's lap and plays a few steps away. When a large dog barks, the child runs back, is held, and after a while goes out to play again.
Step 1: The child leaves the caregiver to explore, and returns to find comfort when anxious.
Step 2: This matches the use of a secure base that Bowlby described.
Interpretation: Attachment is not a string that holds a child back; it is a springboard that makes exploration possible.

examples.title: Choosing a developmental stage
body: Condition (hypothetical): A 10-month-old crawls after the caregiver, crying, when the caregiver leaves the room. The same child at 30 months, hearing "Mom will be back soon, after you finish your snack," nods and goes back to playing.
Step 1: The 10-month-old's behavior matches the clear-cut attachment phase, in which the child seeks a particular person and shows separation anxiety.
Step 2: The 30-month-old's behavior matches the goal-corrected partnership phase, in which the child understands and accepts why the caregiver leaves and when they will return.
Interpretation: Read as a change of stage within the same child, the reduction in distress at separation can be understood not as weakening attachment but as a maturing relationship.

checks.prompt: Arrange Bowlby's stages of attachment development in order.
checks.hint: Everyone, then familiar people, then a particular person, then negotiating, in that order.
checks.explanation: The child moves from sending signals to anyone, through attachment to a particular person, to a reciprocal relationship.

checks.prompt: Match each infant in the figure's records with the attachment type that most closely matches their behavior.
checks.hint: Focus on their behavior when the caregiver returns.
checks.explanation: Ga, who is comforted at reunion and returns to play, shows secure attachment; Na, who avoids the caregiver, shows insecure-avoidant attachment; Da, who approaches yet pushes away, shows insecure-resistant (ambivalent) attachment. In practice, a single observation is not used for judgment.

figure.alt: A table titled "Strange Situation observation records (three hypothetical infants)." The columns are infant, when the caregiver leaves, and when the caregiver returns. Ga: when the caregiver leaves, cries and looks toward the door; when the caregiver returns, approaches and is held, soon calms, and returns to the toys. Na: when the caregiver leaves, keeps playing with no particular reaction; when the caregiver returns, looks away and does not approach. Da: when the caregiver leaves, cries hard; when the caregiver returns, wants to be held yet pushes away, and does not calm for a long time. At the bottom: "A record is a single observation and does not diagnose the child."

checks.prompt: What is the most appropriate evaluation of the claim "A child who does not cry when separated has a secure attachment"?
checks.hint: Think about Na in the figure.
checks.explanation: In the Strange Situation, behavior at reunion is especially important, and not crying alone does not establish secure attachment.
options: True. If there is no crying, it is secure attachment
Not true. Not crying at separation and avoiding the caregiver at reunion is described as a feature of avoidant attachment
True. Attachment types are determined only by reactions at separation
Not true. The Strange Situation does not observe separation scenes

checks.prompt: Which statement about the internal working model is most appropriate?
checks.hint: Think about the expectation "Will other people help me?"
checks.explanation: The internal working model is Bowlby's concept, and it is thought to influence expectations and behavior in later relationships.
options: A framework of expectations about oneself and others, formed through accumulated attachment experiences
The eight-scene observation procedure used in the laboratory
One of the nine dimensions of temperament
A daily schedule of caregiving

ece-12.title: Emotional Development and Emotion Coaching
explain: When a child who has had a toy taken away screams and cries, adults respond in very different ways. Some say "Stop crying, that's enough!" and try to halt the feeling; some ignore it; some give in and let the child have everything; others acknowledge the feeling and find a way forward together. Which response connects with children's emotional development? This lesson looks at the flow of emotional development and at the approach called **emotion coaching** as a theory.

Emotions generally develop in the following flow. In infancy, **basic emotions** such as joy, sadness, anger, and fear appear. From around toddlerhood, as children begin to recognize the self, **self-conscious emotions** such as shame, pride, and guilt appear. In early childhood, children learn to name emotions (emotion vocabulary), guess the causes of others' feelings (emotion understanding), and develop **emotion regulation**, the ability to manage feelings. Emotion regulation begins as **co-regulation**, in which an adult soothes the child, and gradually moves toward **self-regulation**, which the child does on their own.

The American psychologist **Gottman** studied how parents respond to their children's emotions and presented four types.
- **Dismissive type**: treats the child's negative emotions as trivial and quickly changes the subject.
- **Suppressive type**: scolds or punishes the very expression of negative emotions.
- **Permissive type**: accepts all emotions but does not set limits on behavior or help solve problems.
- **Emotion-coaching type**: accepts emotions, sets limits on behavior, and finds solutions together.

Emotion coaching is often summarized in five steps.
1. **Notice** the child's emotion.
2. **Regard the moment the emotion appears as an opportunity** to become closer and to teach.
3. **Accept** the emotion by listening with empathy.
4. Help the child **name the emotion**.
5. **Set limits** on behavior and find ways to solve the problem together.
The key is the distinction that all emotions can be accepted, but not all behaviors. Acknowledge that the child is angry, but make clear that taking a friend's things is not allowed, and find together what can be done instead.

Let us place the five steps on a scene. A block tower collapses and the child throws a block. The teacher goes over, reads the child's expression (noticing), and regards the moment as an opportunity to learn how to handle emotions. The teacher says, "You were upset that the tower fell" (empathy and acceptance), and asks, "Were you upset, and angry too?" to find emotion words together (naming). Next the teacher works on limits and solutions together: "If you throw blocks, a friend could get hurt. How could we make the base wider when we build it again?"

There are limits and cautions as well. Emotion coaching is not a rule that all five steps must be followed at every moment, and dangerous behavior must be stopped first. Expectations about how emotions should be expressed differ among cultures and families, and the emphasis on emotion vocabulary does not carry the same meaning in every culture. Also, this lesson introduces the theory and does not address judgments or treatment of a child's emotional problems, nor serve as guidance for parenting or counseling.

examples.title: Comparing four responses
body: Condition (hypothetical): When playtime ends and the teacher asks the children to tidy up, a child cries, "I want to keep playing!"

Step 1: "Don't cry, it's nothing. I'll give you a sticker instead" is close to the dismissive type; "If you cry, you'll be in trouble" is close to the suppressive type; "Okay, keep playing" is close to the permissive type.

Step 2: "You're sad because you want to keep playing. Tidying up has to be done. Shall we take a photo of the castle you built and continue tomorrow?" accepts the feeling and deals with limits and solutions together, so it is close to the emotion-coaching type.
Interpretation: The two criteria that separate the four types are "Does the response accept the feeling?" and "Does it address the limit on behavior and the solution?"

examples.title: From co-regulation to self-regulation
body: Condition (hypothetical): At age 3, when a child became angry, the teacher held the child and said, "Shall we take a big breath?" The child calmed down only after breathing together. At age 5, when angry, the child goes alone to the quiet book area, sits for a while, and comes back.
Step 1: The 3-year-old's pattern is co-regulation, managing the emotion together with an adult.
Step 2: The 5-year-old's pattern shows the child using a strategy alone, a move to self-regulation.
Interpretation: Repeated experiences of co-regulation form the basis for self-regulation, a flow that resembles the scaffolding in Lesson 9.

checks.prompt: Arrange the five steps of emotion coaching in order.
checks.hint: Notice, then opportunity, then empathy, then naming, then limits and solutions.
checks.explanation: The process is structured so that handling the emotion leads to a solution.
items: Regard it as an opportunity to become closer and to teach
Listen with empathy and accept the emotion
Help the child name the emotion
Set limits and find solutions together

checks.prompt: Match each of Gottman's response types with a statement.
checks.hint: Use two criteria: whether the child's feeling is accepted, and whether limits and solutions are addressed.
checks.explanation: Only the emotion-coaching type addresses acceptance of emotion, limits on behavior, and solutions together.
pairs: "Don't worry about it, let's have a snack instead"
"If you cry like that, you'll be punished"
"You're angry, so you can take your friend's block"
"You're angry. Taking things is not okay. How shall we decide the turns?"

checks.prompt: (Hypothetical case) A teacher says "You were upset, it's all fine" to a child who pushed a friend, and leaves the child as is. From the viewpoint of emotion coaching, which step is missing?
checks.hint: Think about the difference between the permissive type and the emotion-coaching type.
checks.explanation: The feeling was accepted, but the limit and solution for the pushing behavior were not addressed, so this is close to the permissive type.
options: Noticing the emotion
Listening with empathy and accepting the emotion
The fact that the feeling was accepted is the problem
Setting limits on behavior and finding solutions

checks.prompt: Which statement about emotion coaching is NOT consistent with the content of this lesson?
checks.hint: The steps are a framework, not a rule.
checks.explanation: Dangerous behavior must be stopped first, and the five steps are not a rule to be followed at every moment.
options: Accept feelings, but do not accept every behavior
Even when there is dangerous behavior, one must not stop the behavior until all five steps are complete
Expectations about expressing emotions can differ across cultures and families
Emotion regulation tends to move from co-regulation to self-regulation

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain how the emotion-coaching type differs from the dismissive and permissive types, distinguishing between "emotion" and "behavior."
checks.hint: Compare the three types on the two criteria: accepting feelings, and addressing limits and solutions for behavior.
checks.explanation: Handling emotion and behavior separately is the core of emotion coaching.
checks.model: The dismissive type passes over the child's emotion as trivial, and the permissive type accepts the emotion but sets no limits on behavior. The emotion-coaching type accepts and empathizes with the emotion while clearly setting limits on behavior and finding solutions together with the child.

ece-13.title: Parten's Stages of Social Play Development
explain: A classroom's building area has three children stacking blocks. Are they playing together? Being close does not mean playing together. To observe play, a framework is needed that separates "with whom" and "in what kind of relationship" children play. The American researcher **Parten** observed the free play of young children in the 1930s and divided the **levels of social participation** in play into six categories.

Parten's six categories are as follows.
1. **Unoccupied behavior**: not absorbed in any particular play; looks around or wanders.
2. **Onlooker behavior**: watches other children play and may talk to them, but does not join in.
3. **Solitary play**: plays alone with one's own toys, independent of other children.
4. **Parallel play**: plays with similar toys beside other children, but does not exchange or interact; each plays separately.
5. **Associative play**: shares and talks with other children while playing, but there is no clear common goal or division of roles.
6. **Cooperative play**: divides roles and organizes play toward a shared goal, such as a shop or a large castle.

Asking the questions in order makes classification easier. (1) Is the child absorbed in play? If not, the behavior is unoccupied or onlooker behavior; if there is a child being watched, it is onlooker behavior. (2) If the child is playing, are other children doing similar play nearby? If not, it is solitary play. (3) If they are nearby, do they exchange with each other? If not, it is parallel play. (4) If they do exchange, is there a shared goal and a division of roles? If not, it is associative play; if so, cooperative play.

Parten reported that associative and cooperative play tend to increase with age, and these categories were long read as "stages." Later researchers, however, added an important correction. Solitary play is not necessarily immature; for an older child, solitary constructive play may be focused play. Parallel play can also act as a **bridge** into other children's play. It is often observed that children who play similarly beside one another naturally begin to talk and move into associative play.

Observation methods are also worth knowing. Parten's categories are often recorded using time sampling: for example, one child is observed every minute, and one category is marked for that moment. Afterward, the frequency and proportion of each category can be calculated. The proportion is "the number of times marked in that category ÷ total observations × 100."

There are limits too. Parten's observations were made in one kindergarten in a particular era and region, and category distributions may differ when the play environment and culture differ. The same child may show different categories depending on indoor or outdoor settings, the kind of toys, and whether the children playing together are familiar. Therefore, category proportions are used not as scores that rank a child's "level," but as data for understanding what kind of play appears in which situations.

examples.title: Deciding categories with the judging questions
body: Condition (hypothetical): In the sandpit, Eunwoo and Rian sit side by side and each builds their own sandcastle. Eunwoo says, "Look at my castle!" and Rian hands him a shovel. They pass sand to each other and talk, but each builds their own castle.
Step 1: Both children are absorbed in play and are beside each other. Since there is no exchange in the first scene, it is parallel play.
Step 2: They hand over a shovel, talk, and pass sand to each other. There is still no shared castle or division of roles, so it has changed to associative play.
Interpretation: Within a single scene the category can change, and this is an example of parallel play serving as a bridge to associative play.

examples.title: Calculating category proportions
body: Condition (hypothetical): One child was observed 30 times at one-minute intervals: solitary play 6, parallel play 9, associative play 10, cooperative play 3, onlooker behavior 2.
Step 1: Check the total. 6 + 9 + 10 + 3 + 2 = 30.
Step 2: The combined proportion of associative and cooperative play is (10 + 3) ÷ 30 × 100 ≈ 43.3%.
Interpretation: This proportion describes this child on this day, in this environment. If the child were observed again on another day or outdoors, the distribution may differ.

checks.prompt: Arrange Parten's play categories from the least to the most social participation.
checks.hint: Not absorbed, then watching, then alone, then side by side without exchange, then exchanging, then shared roles.
checks.explanation: The categories are arranged in increasing degree of social participation. However, actual development does not proceed only in this order.

checks.prompt: (Hypothetical) A child was observed 25 times at one-minute intervals, and parallel play appeared 7 times. What percentage of the observations was parallel play?
checks.hint: frequency ÷ total × 100

checks.prompt: (Hypothetical case) In the role-play area, three children decide on roles, saying, "You're the customer, I'm the cook, and you're the cashier," and play at a restaurant. Which of Parten's categories fits best?
checks.hint: Check whether there is a shared goal and a division of roles.
checks.explanation: Because they divided roles under the shared goal of running a restaurant, this is cooperative play.
options: Parallel play
Associative play
Onlooker behavior
Cooperative play

checks.prompt: Which evaluation is most appropriate for the claim "If a five-year-old does a lot of solitary play, their social development is delayed"?
checks.hint: Think about the correction that later researchers added.
checks.explanation: The meaning of solitary play depends on its content and situation. Focused, solitary constructive play is not necessarily immature, and category proportions are not used to evaluate children.
options: True. Solitary play is the lowest level, so it is delayed
Not true. Solitary play, such as focused constructive play, does not necessarily mean immaturity; it depends on the situation
True. Parten said solitary play completely disappears by age five
Not true. Solitary play is a higher level than cooperative play

ece-14.title: Smilansky's Cognitive Play and Sociodramatic Play
explain: Lesson 13 looked at play along the axis of "with whom." This lesson adds the axis of "with what kind of thinking." The four types of play we saw in Stage 1 (functional, constructive, symbolic, and rule-based) are nearly the same as the **cognitive play** categories organized by the Israeli researcher **Smilansky** on the basis of Piaget's classification of play. Smilansky called symbolic play **dramatic play**.

Using both axes together allows more precise records of play. The American researcher **Rubin** and colleagues created an observation framework that crosses Parten's social categories with Smilansky's cognitive categories. For example, "parallel-constructive" is building blocks beside another child, each on one's own, and "group-dramatic" is pretend play in which several children take on roles, such as a pretend house. Counting the times in each cell shows at a glance how one child's play looks.

explain.alt: A table titled "Hayul's play sampling, 20 observations (hypothetical)." The rows are alone, parallel, and group; the columns are functional, constructive, dramatic, and rule-based. Alone row: functional 1, constructive 4, dramatic 0, rule 0, total 5. Parallel row: functional 1, constructive 5, dramatic 1, rule 0, total 7. Group row: functional 0, constructive 2, dramatic 5, rule 1, total 8. Column totals: functional 2, constructive 11, dramatic 6, rule 1, overall 20. Below is written: "Rows: Parten's social play (group combines associative and cooperative play)" and "Columns: Smilansky's cognitive play."

explain:
The figure is Hayul's data from 20 samples. The table can be read in the following order.
1. Check the overall total (20).
2. Look at the cognitive distribution through the column totals: constructive 11, dramatic 6, functional 2, rule-based 1, so constructive play is the most frequent.
3. Look at the social distribution through the row totals: alone 5, parallel 7, group 8.
4. Look at the cells. Of the 6 dramatic play observations, 5 occurred in the group row, so Hayul's dramatic play mostly happens together with friends.
5. Convert to proportions. For example, the proportion of constructive play is 11 ÷ 20 × 100 = 55%.

Smilansky paid particular attention to **sociodramatic play**, dramatic play done together with others, and presented six elements for judging its level.
- **Role imitation**: taking on the role of a person and imitating their words and actions.
- **Object substitution**: treating one object as another (a block as a telephone).
- **Behavior and situation pretense**: describing behavior or situations with words ("Now it's night").
- **Persistence**: a play theme continues for a certain time (Smilansky used about 10 minutes or longer as the standard).
- **Interaction**: two or more children relate to each other within the play theme.
- **Verbal communication**: talking with each other about the play ("You're the baby").
The first four elements can also appear in solitary dramatic play; sociodramatic play is formed when the last two elements are added.

There are limits as well. Because the cognitive categories are based on Piaget's theory, observers may disagree about which category an activity belongs in (a block castle with a story: constructive or dramatic?). It is therefore important to agree on the definitions and boundary cases before observing. Also, if sociodramatic play elements are read as a hierarchy of "good play" in which more elements always means better, one may overlook the value of other play the child has chosen.

examples.title: Recording on two axes
body: Condition (hypothetical): (1) Siwoo does a puzzle alone next to a friend. (2) Three children say, "We're firefighters!" and divide roles and pretend to put out a fire. (3) A child rolls a ball and catches it again and again, alone.
Step 1: (1) is socially parallel and cognitively constructive (manipulation), so it is "parallel-constructive."
Step 2: (2) is "group-dramatic," and (3) is "alone-functional."
Interpretation: If only one axis is used, (1) and (3) both look like play done alone, but using both axes shows that they are different kinds of play.

examples.title: Finding sociodramatic play elements
body: Condition (hypothetical): Two children play hospital for 15 minutes. One says, "I'm the doctor, you're the patient," and uses a pencil as a syringe, saying, "Now you've had your shot." The other child says, "Ow," and holds out an arm.
Step 1: Role imitation (doctor and patient), object substitution (a pencil as a syringe), behavior and situation pretense ("now you've had your shot"), and persistence (15 minutes) all appear.
Step 2: The two children form relationships through their roles (interaction), and set the play by talking about it (verbal communication).
Interpretation: All six elements are visible, so this can be read as sociodramatic play.

checks.prompt: Match each sociodramatic play element with a scene.
checks.hint: Distinguish imitating a person, changing an object, creating a situation with words, and talking about the play.
checks.explanation: These four, together with persistence and interaction, make up Smilansky's six elements.
pairs: Pretends to drive a bus, saying, "I'm the bus driver"
Uses one block as a mobile phone
Sets the situation in words, saying, "Now it's raining"
Negotiates, saying, "You be the customer, and I'll be the driver"

ece-15.title: Reggio Emilia: Documentation and Interest-Area Design
explain: When people speak of a play-centered curriculum, a common misunderstanding is that "children should just be left to play." The opposite error, having children follow only the topics and activities the teacher has set in advance, makes children lose interest. The path between these two is presented as the **emergent curriculum**. The curriculum is not fully fixed in advance; it grows out of children's interests and questions, and teachers observe, interpret, and extend it.

A well-known example of the emergent curriculum is the **Reggio Emilia** approach, named after a northern Italian city. It began in early childhood schools founded by local communities after World War II, and was led by the educator **Malaguzzi**. The main ideas are as follows.
- **Capable child**: the child is a capable being who asks questions on their own and builds theories.
- **The hundred languages of children**: children express their thinking in many ways beyond words, such as drawing, clay, gesture, and light and shadow.
- **The environment as the third teacher**: after adults and friends, space and materials influence learning.
- **Projects**: beginning from children's questions, the class explores deeply over several weeks or months.
- **Atelier and atelierista**: some settings have a workshop space for expressive work and a teacher with an arts background.

The core tool of the Reggio approach is **documentation**. Documentation is not simply a display of photos stuck to a wall; it is a cycle that makes children's learning process visible and plans what comes next based on it.
1. **Observation**: watch the child's talk, actions, and work.
2. **Recording**: write down what children say, and gather photos and works.
3. **Interpretation**: read the records together with colleagues and guess at the child's questions and thinking.
4. **Planning**: prepare materials, questions, and space based on the interpretation.
5. **Sharing**: share the records with children and families, and let children revisit their own process.
New responses from children that emerge in sharing lead back to observation.

This idea connects to the design of interest areas in Lesson 4 of Stage 1. In the emergent curriculum, interest areas are not fixed boxes but spaces that change according to how the documentation is interpreted. For example, if children show interest in shadows, a light table, flashlights, and transparent colored sheets might be placed on one side of the book area to open a new "light and shadow area." When changing materials, the principles of the nature of activities, traffic flow, accessibility, and flexibility from Stage 1 are also considered.

Being emergent does not mean that the teacher disappears. Teachers choose what to document, interpret it, and actively widen the play through materials and questions. The scaffolding of Lesson 9 is used in this process. Korea's 2019 Revised Nuri Curriculum also emphasizes child-centered, play-centered education, and values the teacher's role in observing and supporting play.

There are also limits and debates. The Reggio approach grew out of the history and community culture of a particular region, so it is often pointed out that it is difficult to transplant directly. Reggio itself has also introduced its work not as a "model" to copy but as an ongoing "experience" to study. There is further critical discussion that documentation takes much time and coordination, and that records must be careful not to become surveillance of children or display-only posters. When sharing a child's photos and words, respect for the privacy of the child and family is required.

examples.title: The documentation cycle of a shadow project
body: Condition (hypothetical): During outdoor play, one child shouted, "My shadow is following me!" and several children ran around trying to step on their shadows.
Step 1 (observation and recording): The teacher wrote down the children's words ("In the morning the shadow is long," "When the clouds come, it disappears") and took photos.

Step 2 (interpretation and planning): The teacher read the records with a colleague and interpreted them as showing that the children are curious about the relationship between shadow length and light. Indoors, they prepared a light and shadow area with flashlights and a light table.

Interpretation: During sharing, the records were pinned to the wall and viewed together with the children. One child said, "If you bring the flashlight closer, it gets bigger!" This new discovery led back to observation.

examples.title: Redesigning an interest area
body: Condition (hypothetical): The records show that during shop play in the role-play area, children keep taking blocks from the building area to use as "goods," moving back and forth between the two areas and crossing other children's play.
Step 1: The flow of the play (the shop needs goods) and the spatial arrangement (the two areas are far apart) do not match.
Step 2: Add open materials such as boxes and bottle caps to the role-play area, or place the two areas closer together to shorten the traffic path.
Interpretation: Viewing the environment as the "third teacher" means continually reorganizing spaces and materials based on records of children's play.

checks.prompt: Arrange the steps of the documentation cycle in order.
checks.hint: Observe, record, read together, plan, and share.
checks.explanation: The response that emerges from sharing leads back to observation, forming a cycle.

checks.prompt: Match each concept of the Reggio Emilia approach with its meaning.
checks.hint: Think about whether each concept concerns children, space, inquiry, or records.
checks.explanation: The four concepts together form the emergent curriculum.

The environment as the third teacher
Starting from children's questions and inquiring deeply over a long period
Making the learning process visible and using it as the basis for the next plan

checks.prompt: (Hypothetical case) For several days, children have been observing ants and asking, "Where do ants sleep?" From the viewpoint of the emergent curriculum, what is the teacher's most appropriate next action?
checks.hint: Think about the flow of observation, recording, interpretation, and planning.
checks.explanation: In the emergent curriculum, the teacher records and interprets the children's interests and expands them with materials and questions.

Prepare nothing and let the children work it out on their own
Show a video that explains the answer and end the topic
Record the children's questions and talk, discuss them with a colleague, and then prepare materials such as magnifying glasses and picture books to broaden the inquiry

checks.hint: Does the word "emergent" mean that the teacher disappears?
checks.explanation: Teachers actively take part by recording, interpreting, and expanding the play through materials and questions.
options: The teacher drops out of children's play and does not intervene at all
It grew out of the history and community culture of a particular region
It has been pointed out that documentation takes much time and coordination
It views children as capable beings who ask questions on their own

checks.prompt: The claim "If the Reggio Emilia approach's methods are copied as they are, the same results will follow in any country." What is the most appropriate evaluation?
checks.hint: Think about issues of context and culture.
checks.explanation: Reggio itself introduced its approach as an experience to study, not a model to copy, and many point out that it grew from regional history and community culture and is hard to transplant directly.
options: True. Copying documentation alone is enough
True. Reggio presents itself as a fixed model
Not true. It is pointed out that it grew from regional history and community culture and is hard to transplant directly
Not true. The Reggio approach forbids play

ece-16.title: Refining Observation Methods: Sampling and Interobserver Agreement
explain: Two teachers watched the same child at the same time. One recorded "often speaks to friends," and the other recorded "hardly speaks." Which should be trusted? For observation to serve as evidence for understanding a child, we must be able to check its **reliability**, that is, whether others watching the same scene would record it similarly. This lesson refines the observation methods introduced in Stage 1.

Observation methods are distinguished by what they record and how much detail they capture.
- **Anecdotal record**: a brief narrative of one scene judged meaningful, focusing on facts. It is rich in context, but the observer's view enters through the choice of what to record.
- **Time sampling**: at fixed time intervals, marks whether the target behavior appeared. The frequency and proportion can be known, but the context before and after the behavior is lost.
- **Event sampling**: records each time the target behavior (for example, a quarrel) occurs. It is often done in the **ABC format**, dividing the antecedent event (A), the behavior (B), and the consequence (C), to see the context of the behavior.
- **Checklists and rating scales**: mark the presence or degree of predetermined items.

Some things must be decided in advance to use time sampling. (1) **Operational definition of the target behavior**: define "talks to peers" in observable terms, such as "begins speaking while looking at another child." (2) **Interval and number**: for example, every minute, for 10 times. (3) **Marking method**: O if present, - if absent. Then the **rate of occurrence** is calculated as "number of intervals marked ÷ total number of intervals × 100."

explain: The simplest way to check reliability is **interobserver agreement**. Two observers record the same child separately, and then the marks in each cell are compared to see whether they match. Agreement is calculated as "number of agreeing cells ÷ total cells × 100." By comparing the rows of Observer A and Observer B cell by cell in the figure, you can count how many cells the two marks differ in. Note that cells where both marked - (behavior absent) are also counted as agreement. In general, when agreement is low, first check whether the operational definition of the target behavior was ambiguous.

There are also limitations. Simple agreement does not subtract the probability that two people mark the same thing by chance, so when a behavior is very rare or very frequent, agreement can be inflated. Some studies use corrected indices. Also, high agreement means the two people recorded similarly, not that the record accurately captured the child's behavior (validity). The observation methods here are theoretical tools for understanding children and are not used to diagnose them.

examples.title: ABC recording in event sampling
body: Condition (hypothetical): Each time a quarrel occurred in the building area, it was recorded. Event 1: the space was narrow, and two children's towers bumped together (A), then one child pushed the friend's tower (B), and both towers collapsed and both children cried (C).

Step 2: If only the behavior is seen, a "pushing child" appears; looking at A reveals the arrangement of space as a repeated trigger.

Interpretation: ABC recording in event sampling allows one to look at context and environment rather than attributing the behavior only to the child. Adjusting the environment, such as widening the space, can be considered first.

ece-17.title: Portfolio Assessment and Play-Based Assessment
explain: Can a single worksheet or a single observation reveal a young child's learning? Early childhood is a time when a child's appearance changes greatly from day to day depending on condition and circumstance, and written tests do not suit children of this age. For this reason, early childhood education emphasizes assessment that collects materials over time from everyday play and activities in order to understand learning. This kind of assessment is often called **authentic assessment**, and its representative tool is the **portfolio**.

A **portfolio** is a systematic collection, over a certain period, of a child's works, photos, observation records, and words. What distinguishes it from simply stored files is that it **selects materials according to purpose**, records **why each item was chosen and what it shows**, and arranges them to show **change** over time.

The process of making a portfolio can be summarized as follows.
1. **Setting the purpose**: what is to be understood (for example, changes in drawing expression, or communication with friends).
2. **Collecting**: gather works, photos, anecdotal records, and sampling records by date.
3. **Selecting**: choose meaningful materials in light of the purpose and write down the reasons.
4. **Reflecting**: look at the materials together with the child, listen to the child's thinking ("How did you make this?"), and add the teacher's interpretation.
5. **Sharing**: share with the family, and plan the next play support.

The portfolio connects with the earlier lessons. The documentation of Lesson 15 makes visible the learning process of the whole class, while the portfolio makes visible the learning flow of one child. The sampling records and anecdotal records of Lesson 16 become material for the portfolio, and the child's drawings and words fill in the gaps. When materials from many days and many methods point in the same direction, the interpretation becomes more solid. Comparing materials from several sources in this way is sometimes called **triangulation**.

There are also principles to follow in assessment.
- **Change rather than comparison**: compare the same child's earlier appearance, not other children.
- **Strengths rather than deficits**: look first at what the child can now do and what interests them, rather than a list of what they cannot do.
- **The child's voice**: give the child opportunities to talk about their works and processes.
- **Distinguishing fact from interpretation**: apply the principle from Lesson 5 of Stage 1 to portfolio notes as well.

There are also limitations. Portfolios take much time, and the teacher's expectations can enter into what is selected, which raises questions of objectivity. If materials accumulate without being turned into interpretation and plans, the portfolio becomes a "pretty album." Also, a child's photos and words are personal information, so their storage and sharing require care. This lesson is a theory for understanding assessment and does not cover tools for screening or diagnosing children.

examples.title: Portfolio of changes in drawing expression
body: Condition (hypothetical): The purpose is "changes in how the child draws people." Three drawings of people, made in March, June, and September, were collected, along with the words the child said while drawing.

Step 1 (selection): The March drawing shows a circle with lines attached; June shows a body with arms and legs separated; September shows clothes and fingers. The teacher chose the three drawings and wrote down the dates and the reasons.
Step 2 (reflection): Looking at the September drawing, the child said, "This is me running with my friend." The teacher separately wrote the interpretation, "Begins to put stories into drawings."

Interpretation: Rather than comparing with other children's drawings, the teacher looks at the same child's change, and next time can prepare materials that continue a story into drawings (long paper, continuous panels).

examples.title: Strengthening interpretation through triangulation
body: Condition (hypothetical): The teacher guessed, "Seoyun is very interested in counting numbers."
Step 1: Gather an anecdotal record (counting and handing out cups at snack time), a work (a price tag with numbers in the shop play), and the child's words ("I can count to ten!").
Step 2: The three sources point in the same direction, so the interpretation became more solid.
Interpretation: If there had been only one source, it could have been an accidental scene. Comparing several sources is the strength of portfolio assessment.
